items.stem: Let f: [0, ∞) → [0, ∞) be a differentiable function with f(x) > 0 for all x > 0, and f(0) = 0. Further, f satisfies (f(x))² = ∫₀ˣ ((f(t))² + f(t)) dt, x > 0. Then which one of the following options is correct?
items.explanation: Differentiate both sides (fundamental theorem of calculus): 2f(x)f′(x) = f(x)² + f(x). For x > 0, f(x) > 0, so divide by f: f′ = (f + 1)/2. Then d/dx ln(f + 1) = 1/2, so ln(f + 1) = x/2 + c, and f(0) = 0 gives c = 0. Hence f(x) = e^(x/2) − 1 and f(2) = e − 1 ≈ 1.718, which lies in (1, 2].

items.stem: Among the following four statements about countability and uncountability of different sets, which is the correct statement?
options: The set ⋃ₙ₌₀^∞ {x ∈ ℝ : x = Σᵢ₌₀ⁿ 10ⁱ aᵢ, where aᵢ ∈ {1, 2} for i = 0, 1, 2, …, n} is uncountable
The set {x ∈ (0, 1) : x = Σₙ₌₁^∞ aₙ/10ⁿ, where aₙ = 1 or 2 for each n ∈ ℕ} is uncountable
There exists an uncountable set whose elements are pairwise disjoint open intervals in ℝ
The set of all intervals with rational end points is uncountable
items.explanation: The first set is a countable union of finite sets (each n gives 2ⁿ⁺¹ integers), so it is countable. The second set is every infinite sequence of digits from {1, 2}; distinct sequences give distinct numbers, and such sequences are as many as the binary sequences, so it is uncountable. Disjoint open intervals each contain a different rational, so there are at most countably many. Intervals with rational end points are indexed by pairs of rationals, a countable set.

items.stem: Let S = {(x, y, z) ∈ ℝ³ \ {(0, 0, 0)} : z = −(x + y)}. Denote S⊥ = {(p, q, r) ∈ ℝ³ : px + qy + rz = 0 for all (x, y, z) ∈ S}. Then which one of the following options is correct?
options: S⊥ is not a subspace of ℝ³
items.explanation: S is the plane x + y + z = 0 with the origin removed; it still spans that plane, which has dimension 2. The vectors orthogonal to the plane form its normal line, spanned by (1, 1, 1). So S⊥ is a subspace of dimension 3 − 2 = 1.

items.stem: Let I = π² ∫₀¹ ∫₀¹ y² cos π(1 + xy) dx dy. The value of I is equal to ________ (answer in integer).
items.explanation: cos(π + πxy) = −cos(πxy). Integrate in x first: ∫₀¹ cos(πxy) dx = sin(πy)/(πy). So I = −π² ∫₀¹ y² sin(πy)/(πy) dy = −π ∫₀¹ y sin(πy) dy. By parts, ∫₀¹ y sin(πy) dy = [−y cos(πy)/π]₀¹ + ∫₀¹ cos(πy)/π dy = 1/π + 0. Hence I = −π × (1/π) = −1.
items.check: The integrand y² cos π(1 + xy) is negative wherever xy < 1/2, so a negative answer is expected.

items.stem: Let P = [[1, 2], [−1, 4]] and Q = P³ − 2P² − 4P + 13I₂, where I₂ denotes the identity matrix of order 2. Then the determinant of Q is equal to ________ (answer in integer).
items.explanation: P has trace 5 and determinant 4 + 2 = 6, so its eigenvalues are the roots of λ² − 5λ + 6: λ = 2 and 3. Q = q(P) with q(λ) = λ³ − 2λ² − 4λ + 13 has eigenvalues q(2) = 8 − 8 − 8 + 13 = 5 and q(3) = 27 − 18 − 12 + 13 = 10. det Q = 5 × 10 = 50.
items.check: det Q is the product of q at the eigenvalues of P; both are positive, so det Q > 0.

items.stem: Let T: ℝ³ → ℝ³ be a linear map defined by T(x₁, x₂, x₃) = (3x₁ + 5x₂ + x₃, x₃, 2x₁ + 2x₃). Then the rank of T is equal to ________ (answer in integer).
items.explanation: The matrix of T has rows (3, 5, 1), (0, 0, 1), (2, 0, 2). Expanding along the second row: det = −1 × det[[3, 5], [2, 0]] = −1 × (0 − 10) = 10 ≠ 0. A non-zero determinant means full rank, 3.
items.check: The rank of a 3 × 3 matrix is at most 3, and it is 3 exactly when the determinant is non-zero.

items.stem: Let ℱ = {f: [a, b] → ℝ | f is continuous on [a, b] and differentiable on (a, b)}. Which one of the following options is correct?
options: There exists a non-constant f ∈ ℱ such that |f(x) − f(y)| ≤ |x − y|² for all x, y ∈ [a, b]
If f ∈ ℱ and x₀ ∈ (a, b), then there exist distinct x₁, x₂ ∈ [a, b] such that (f(x₁) − f(x₂))/(x₁ − x₂) = f′(x₀)
Let f ∈ ℱ and f′(x) ≥ 0 for all x ∈ (a, b). If f′ is zero only at two distinct points, then f is strictly increasing
Let f ∈ ℱ. If f′(x₁) < c < f′(x₂) for some x₁, x₂ ∈ (a, b), then there may NOT exist an x₀ ∈ (x₁, x₂) such that f′(x₀) = c
items.explanation: If f′ ≥ 0 and f′ vanishes only at two points, then for x < y the mean value theorem on small pieces avoiding those points shows f(y) − f(x) > 0, so f is strictly increasing. The other three fail. |f(x) − f(y)| ≤ |x − y|² forces f′ = 0 everywhere, so f is constant. For f(x) = x³ on [−1, 1] and x₀ = 0, a secant of slope f′(0) = 0 would need f(x₁) = f(x₂) with x₁ ≠ x₂, impossible for a strictly increasing function. Darboux's theorem says derivatives have the intermediate value property, so such an x₀ always exists.

items.stem: Let U = {(x, y) ∈ ℝ² : x + y ≤ 2}. Define f: U → ℝ by f(x, y) = (x − 1)⁴ + (y − 2)⁴. The minimum value of f over U is
items.explanation: The unconstrained minimum is at (1, 2), but 1 + 2 = 3 > 2, so it is outside U and the minimum lies on the line x + y = 2. Put u = x − 1 and v = y − 2; then u + v = −1 and we minimise u⁴ + v⁴. By symmetry and convexity the minimum is at u = v = −1/2 (Lagrange: 4u³ = 4v³ gives u = v), with value 2 × (1/2)⁴ = 1/8.

items.stem: Let P = (aᵢⱼ) be a 10 × 10 matrix with aᵢⱼ = −1/10 if i ≠ j and aᵢⱼ = 9/10 if i = j. Then rank(P) equals
items.explanation: P = I − (1/10)J, where J is the all-ones matrix. J has eigenvalue 10 once (eigenvector 1) and 0 nine times, so P has eigenvalue 1 − 1 = 0 once and 1 nine times. P is symmetric, so its rank is the number of non-zero eigenvalues: 9. (P is the centring matrix: P1 = 0.)

items.stem: Let {xₙ}ₙ≥₁ be a sequence defined as xₙ = 1 + 1/√2 + 1/√3 + ⋯ + 1/√n − 2(√n − 1). Then which of the following options is/are correct?
statements: The sequence {xₙ}ₙ≥₁ is bounded but does not converge
items.explanation: Each step adds 1/√(n + 1) but subtracts 2(√(n + 1) − √n) = 2/(√(n + 1) + √n), which is larger, so xₙ decreases. The integral comparison Σₖ₌₁ⁿ 1/√k ≥ ∫₁ⁿ⁺¹ dx/√x = 2√(n + 1) − 2 keeps xₙ above 2(√(n + 1) − √n) > 0, so it is bounded below and converges (to 2 + ζ(1/2) ≈ 0.54).

A.why: False: it is decreasing and bounded below (see the reasons for B and D).

C.why: False: a bounded monotone sequence converges.

D.why: Comparing with ∫ dx/√x, Σₖ≤ₙ 1/√k − 2√n stays above −2 + 1 > −∞, so xₙ is decreasing and bounded below, hence convergent.

items.stem: Let 𝒪 = {P : P is a 3 × 3 real matrix satisfying PᵀP = I₃ and det(P) = 1}, where I₃ denotes the identity matrix of order 3. Then which of the following options is/are correct?
statements: There exists a P ∈ 𝒪 with λ = 1/2 as an eigen value
There exists a P ∈ 𝒪 with λ = 2 as an eigen value
If λ is the only real eigen value of P ∈ 𝒪, then λ = 1
There exists a P ∈ 𝒪 with λ = −1 as an eigen value
items.explanation: Matrices in 𝒪 are rotations of ℝ³. They preserve length, so real eigenvalues are ±1, and the product of the three eigenvalues is det P = 1, which forces the eigenvalue 1 (the rotation axis). A half-turn has eigenvalues 1, −1, −1.

A.why: False: an orthogonal matrix preserves length, so every eigenvalue has |λ| = 1.

B.why: False: for the same reason |λ| = 1, so 2 is impossible.

C.why: True: the eigenvalues are 1 and a pair e^(±iθ), or real ±1 values with product 1; a real eigenvalue of a rotation in 3D is always 1 (the axis), so if only one real value appears it is 1.

D.why: True: rotation by π about an axis, diag(1, −1, −1), has determinant 1 and eigenvalue −1.

items.stem: Let f: ℝ² → ℝ be defined as f(x, y) = x²y² + 8x − 4y. The number of saddle points of f is ________ (answer in integer).
items.explanation: Critical points solve f_x = 2xy² + 8 = 0 and f_y = 2x²y − 4 = 0. The second gives y = 2/x²; substituting, 8/x³ + 8 = 0, so x = −1 and y = 2: one critical point. There f_xx = 2y² = 8, f_yy = 2x² = 2, f_xy = 4xy = −8, and f_xx f_yy − f_xy² = 16 − 64 < 0, so it is a saddle point.
items.check: A saddle point must first be a critical point; there is only one, so the answer is 0 or 1.

items.stem: Let P be the 5 × 5 matrix with rows (0, 1, 1, 1, 1), (−1, 0, 1, 1, 1), (−1, −1, 0, 1, 1), (−1, −1, −1, 0, 1), (−1, −1, −1, −1, 0). If λ₁, λ₂, λ₃, λ₄, and λ₅ are eigen values of P, then ∏ᵢ₌₁⁵ λᵢ equals ________ (answer in integer).
items.explanation: The product of the eigenvalues is det P. P is skew-symmetric (Pᵀ = −P), so det P = det(Pᵀ) = det(−P) = (−1)⁵ det P = −det P, which forces det P = 0.
items.check: Every odd-order skew-symmetric matrix is singular; check that Pᵀ = −P before computing anything.

items.stem: Let P = [[2, 1], [1, 2]] and Q = [[1, 1], [−2, 4]]. Then the value of trace(P⁵ + Q⁴) equals ________ (answer in integer).
items.explanation: Trace of a power is the sum of the eigenvalues' powers. P has eigenvalues 1 and 3 (trace 4, determinant 3), so trace(P⁵) = 1 + 243 = 244. Q has trace 5 and determinant 4 + 2 = 6, so eigenvalues 2 and 3 and trace(Q⁴) = 16 + 81 = 97. Total 244 + 97 = 341.
items.check: trace(P⁵) alone is dominated by 3⁵ = 243 and trace(Q⁴) by 3⁴ = 81, so the answer must exceed 324.
